---
title: "1978 and the Passing Revolution (1978–1999)"
subtitle: "Two rule changes in one spring, and the twenty-year arms race they started."
description: "How the NFL's 1978 rules (the Mel Blount rule and open-hand pass blocking) ended the 1970s scoring drought, and how each side answered the other for two decades: Air Coryell and the West Coast offense, nickel and dime, Arnsparger's 53 and the 3-4, Lawrence Taylor and the blind-side tackle, Gibbs's one-back offense and counter trey against Buddy Ryan's 46, the run-and-shoot and the K-Gun, the zone blitz, the 1994 rule package (two-point conversion, kickoffs from the 30), and the free agency (1993) and salary cap (1994) that changed how every roster was built."
glossary:
  "Mel Blount rule (1978)": {def: "The 1978 NFL rule that lets a defender contact a receiver only within five yards of the line of scrimmage while the quarterback still has the ball; beyond five yards, contact that impedes the receiver is a foul (today called illegal contact). Named for the Pittsburgh cornerback whose physical coverage helped prompt it.", aliases: ["Mel Blount rule"]}
  "53 defense": "Bill Arnsparger's package for the early-1970s Miami Dolphins, named for linebacker Bob Matheson's jersey number: Matheson lined up at the end of the line and either rushed like a fourth defensive lineman or dropped like a fourth linebacker, so the same eleven players could be a 4-3 or a 3-4 from one snap to the next. Usually named as an NFL ancestor of the 3-4."
  "Blind-side tackle": "The offensive tackle who protects the side a quarterback cannot see as he sets to throw: the left tackle for a right-handed passer, the right tackle for a left-hander. Since the 1980s teams have treated it as the premium position on the offensive line."
  "Free agency (1993)": "The system, in force in the NFL since March 1, 1993, that lets a veteran whose contract has expired sign with any team (today, after four accrued seasons). An accrued season is one in which the player was on full pay status for at least six regular-season games; a player with three is a restricted free agent, whose old team can keep him by matching an offer, and one with fewer than three is an exclusive-rights free agent, who can negotiate only with his old team if it tenders him. The system came out of the January 1993 settlement of the players' antitrust lawsuits."
  "Salary cap": "A hard limit, the same for every team, on what a club may count against its player payroll in a season, set each year from a share of league revenue. The NFL's began in 1994 at $34.6 million per team."

```{python}
#| code-summary: "Show the Python (shared helpers for this chapter's diagrams)"

import logging
logging.getLogger("matplotlib.font_manager").setLevel(logging.ERROR)
import io
import os
import numpy as np
import pandas as pd
import matplotlib.pyplot as plt
from matplotlib.patches import Circle, Ellipse, FancyArrowPatch, Rectangle, RegularPolygon, Wedge
from gridiron import Play, Player, Field, offense, technique, style, routes as r

style.apply()
GREEN = "#0f7a55"         # darker step of the aqua highlight, for text on the light field
PURPLE = style.SERIES[6]  # a ring colour that is neither offense blue nor defense orange
OL_KEYS = ("LT", "LG", "C", "RG", "RT")


def pdf_build():
    return os.environ.get("RTG_FORMAT", "").lower() in ("pdf", "typst", "print")


def O(key, pos, d, w, label):
    return Player(key, pos, "off", d, w, label=label)


def D(key, pos, d, w, label):
    return Player(key, pos, "def", d, w, label=label)


def line(labels="full"):
    """The five offensive linemen, labelled LT..RT ("full") or with one letter, T G C G T ("short")."""
    short = {"LT": "T", "LG": "G", "C": "C", "RG": "G", "RT": "T"}
    return [p.moved(label=(p.key if labels == "full" else short[p.key])) for p in offense("singleback")
            if p.key in OL_KEYS]


def T(t, side=1):
    """Width of technique t on the offense's right (side=+1) or left (side=-1)."""
    return technique(t, side)


def go_to(p, key, end, kind="block", delay=0.0, speed=None, via=()):
    """Move `key` through absolute (d, w) points `via` to `end`, as a block, pull, path, run, rush or route."""
    start = np.array(p._cur(key))
    pts = [tuple(np.array(q) - start) for q in (*via, end)]
    if kind == "block":
        return p.block(key, pts=pts, delay=delay, speed=speed)
    if kind == "pull":
        return p.pull(key, pts, delay=delay, speed=speed)
    if kind == "rush":
        return p.rush(key, pts=pts, delay=delay, speed=speed)
    if kind == "route":
        return p.route(key, [tuple(q) for q in (*via, end)], absolute=True, delay=delay, speed=speed)
    return {"path": p.path, "run": p.run}[kind](key, pts, delay=delay, speed=speed)


def _P(fld, p, d, w):
    return fld.xy(*p.to_abs(d, w))


def say(fld, p, d, w, text, color=style.INK_2, fontsize=7.5, ha="center", weight="normal", alpha=0.9):
    """A short on-field label at (d, w)."""
    x, y = _P(fld, p, d, w)
    fld.ax.text(x, y, text, fontsize=fontsize, color=color, ha=ha, va="center", zorder=9, fontweight=weight,
                bbox=dict(boxstyle="round,pad=0.18", fc=style.SURFACE, ec="none", alpha=alpha))


def point_to(fld, p, text_at, target, text, color=style.INK_2, fontsize=7, shrink=7):
    """A label with a thin leader line to the player or spot it names."""
    (xt, yt), (xp, yp) = _P(fld, p, *text_at), _P(fld, p, *target)
    fld.ax.annotate(text, (float(xp), float(yp)), xytext=(float(xt), float(yt)), fontsize=fontsize,
                    color=color, ha="center", va="center", zorder=9,
                    arrowprops=dict(arrowstyle="-", color=color, lw=0.7, shrinkA=2, shrinkB=shrink),
                    bbox=dict(boxstyle="round,pad=0.18", fc=style.SURFACE, ec="none", alpha=0.9))


def spot(fld, p, d, w, color=style.DEFENSE_DARK, ms=10, marker="X"):
    """Mark a point (a hit, a tackle) with an X."""
    x, y = _P(fld, p, d, w)
    fld.ax.plot([x], [y], marker=marker, ms=ms, color=color, mec="white", mew=0.8, zorder=12)


def ring(fld, p, key, color=GREEN, r=1.25, lw=1.8, ls="-"):
    """A ring around a player at his alignment."""
    q = p.players[key]
    x, y = _P(fld, p, q.d, q.w)
    fld.ax.add_patch(Circle((float(x), float(y)), r, fc="none", ec=color, lw=lw, ls=ls, zorder=7.5))


def band(fld, p, d0, d1, w0, w1, color=GREEN, alpha=0.10, ls=(0, (3, 2)), lw=0.9):
    """Shade a rectangle from depth d0 to d1 and width w0 to w1 (alignment yards)."""
    (x0, y0), (x1, y1) = _P(fld, p, d0, w0), _P(fld, p, d1, w1)
    fld.ax.add_patch(Rectangle((min(x0, x1), min(y0, y1)), abs(x1 - x0), abs(y1 - y0), fc=color, alpha=alpha,
                               ec=color, lw=lw, ls=ls, zorder=0.8))


def dashed(fld, p, pts, color=style.THIRD, lw=1.5, dash=(0, (3, 2.2)), end="arrow"):
    """A dashed 'option' or 'intent' path through absolute (d, w) points."""
    xs, ys = _P(fld, p, np.array([q[0] for q in pts]), np.array([q[1] for q in pts]))
    xs, ys = np.asarray(xs, float), np.asarray(ys, float)
    if end == "arrow":
        hx, hy = xs[-2] + 0.75 * (xs[-1] - xs[-2]), ys[-2] + 0.75 * (ys[-1] - ys[-2])
        xs = np.concatenate([xs[:-1], [hx, xs[-1]]]); ys = np.concatenate([ys[:-1], [hy, ys[-1]]])
        fld.ax.plot(xs[:-1], ys[:-1], color=color, lw=lw, ls=dash, zorder=6)
        fld.ax.add_patch(FancyArrowPatch((xs[-2], ys[-2]), (xs[-1], ys[-1]), arrowstyle="-|>",
                                         mutation_scale=10, color=color, lw=lw, zorder=6))
    else:
        fld.ax.plot(xs, ys, color=color, lw=lw, ls=dash, zorder=6)


def clean(ax, numbers=True):
    """Drop hash ticks (and optionally yard numbers); clip text to the window."""
    for ln in list(ax.lines):
        xs, ys = ln.get_data()
        if len(xs) == 2 and ln.get_linewidth() == 0.5 and np.hypot(xs[1] - xs[0], ys[1] - ys[0]) < 1.0:
            ln.remove()
    for t in list(ax.texts):
        if numbers and t.get_text().isdigit() and t.get_alpha() == 0.55:
            t.remove()
        else:
            t.set_clip_on(True)


def draw(p, width_in=6.2, ax=None, numbers=True, **kw):
    """Play.draw, sized for the page, cleaned for a zoomed window."""
    fld = p.draw(width_in=width_in, ax=ax, **kw)
    clean(fld.ax, numbers=numbers)
    return fld


def ruler(fld, p, depths=(5, 10, 15, 20, 25), w=None, fs=6.5):
    """Depth labels (yards past the line of scrimmage) along the left edge of the window."""
    ax = fld.ax
    x_left = (160 / 3) - fld.y1 + 0.4
    for d in depths:
        y = p.los + d
        if fld.x0 + 0.8 <= y <= fld.x1 - 0.8:
            ax.text(x_left, y, f"{d}" + (" yd" if d == depths[0] else ""), fontsize=fs, color=style.INK_2,
                    ha="left", va="center", zorder=12,
                    bbox=dict(boxstyle="round,pad=0.12", fc=style.SURFACE, ec="none", alpha=0.85))


def title(ax, text, size=9):
    ax.set_title(text, fontsize=size, loc="left", color=style.INK, fontweight="bold")


# --- frame strips (PDF) and video (web) for simulated plays ------------------------------------------
MARK_R = 0.62


def tracking(play):
    df = play.to_tracking()
    df["_id"] = df["displayName"].astype(str)
    return df


def panel(ax, play, df, t, lateral, window, rings=(), ring_r=0.85):
    """One moment of a simulated play on `ax`: markers, trails, rings."""
    tmap = df.groupby("frameId")["time"].first()
    fid = int((tmap - t).abs().idxmin())
    ylo, yhi = sorted((play.ball_y - lateral[0], play.ball_y - lateral[1]))
    fld = Field(ax=ax, orient="vertical", los=play.los, window=window, numbers=False, hashes=False,
                lateral=(ylo, yhi), to_go=play.to_go)
    cur = df[df["frameId"] == fid]
    shown = cur[cur["x"].between(play.los + window[0] + 0.5, play.los + window[1] - 0.5)
                & cur["y"].between(ylo + 0.5, yhi - 0.5) | (cur["side"] == "ball")]
    ids = set(shown["_id"])
    trails = df[(df["frameId"] <= fid) & df["_id"].isin(ids) & (df["side"] != "ball")]
    for (_, side), g in trails.groupby(["_id", "side"]):
        xs, ys = fld.xy(g["x"].values, g["y"].values)
        ax.plot(xs, ys, color=style.OFFENSE if side == "off" else style.DEFENSE, lw=0.9, alpha=0.4, zorder=3)
    ppy = fld.pts_per_yard()
    for _, r_ in shown.iterrows():
        x, y = (float(v) for v in fld.xy(r_["x"], r_["y"]))
        if r_["side"] == "ball":
            ax.add_patch(Ellipse((x, y + 0.45), 0.7, 0.42, fc=style.BALL, ec="white", lw=0.5, zorder=9))
            continue
        lab = str(r_.get("label", "") or "")
        if r_["side"] == "off":
            ax.add_patch(Circle((x, y), MARK_R, fc=style.OFFENSE, ec="white", lw=0.6, zorder=8))
            tc = "white"
        else:
            ax.add_patch(RegularPolygon((x, y), 4, radius=MARK_R * 1.3, orientation=np.pi / 4,
                                        fc=style.DEFENSE_TINT, ec=style.DEFENSE, lw=1.0, zorder=8))
            tc = style.INK
        fs = max(4.0, min(8.0, ppy * (0.85 if len(lab) <= 1 else 0.62)))
        ax.text(x, y, lab, ha="center", va="center", fontsize=fs, color=tc, fontweight="bold", zorder=10)
    for key, col in rings:
        r_ = cur[cur["displayName"] == key].iloc[0]
        x, y = fld.xy(r_["x"], r_["y"])
        ax.add_patch(Circle((float(x), float(y)), ring_r, fc="none", ec=col, lw=1.6, zorder=7))
    for patch in ax.patches:
        patch.set_clip_on(True)
    return fld


def strip(moments, lateral, window, notes=None, rings=(), ncols=2, width_in=6.2, after=None):
    """Numbered frame strip. `moments` is a list of (play, t, tag)."""
    cache = {}
    nrows = int(np.ceil(len(moments) / ncols))
    pw = width_in / ncols
    span_w, span_d = lateral[1] - lateral[0], window[1] - window[0]
    fig, axes = plt.subplots(nrows, ncols, squeeze=False,
                             figsize=(width_in, nrows * (pw * span_d / span_w + (0.75 if notes else 0.25))))
    for ax in axes.flat[len(moments):]:
        ax.axis("off")
    for i, (ax, (play, t, tag)) in enumerate(zip(axes.flat, moments)):
        if id(play) not in cache:
            cache[id(play)] = tracking(play)
        fld = panel(ax, play, cache[id(play)], t, lateral, window, rings)
        if after:
            after(fld, play, t, i)
        lab = "snap" if abs(t) < 1e-6 else f"{t:+.1f} s"
        ax.set_title(f"{i + 1}.  {lab}" + (f"   {tag}" if tag else ""), fontsize=8.3, color=style.INK_2, loc="left")
        if notes:
            ax.text(0.5, -0.03, notes[i], transform=ax.transAxes, ha="center", va="top",
                    fontsize=7.1, color=style.INK)
    fig.tight_layout(h_pad=1.3 if notes else 0.6, w_pad=0.6)
    return fig


def video(play, notes, lateral, window, rings=(), width_in=4.8, after=None):
    """Web version: the play frame by frame, with each moment's note shown as the caption."""
    import shutil
    from matplotlib import animation
    from IPython.display import HTML, display
    span_w, span_d = lateral[1] - lateral[0], window[1] - window[0]
    fig, ax = plt.subplots(figsize=(width_in, width_in * span_d / span_w + 0.5))
    df = tracking(play)
    tmap = df.groupby("frameId")["time"].first()
    frames = [float(tmap[f]) for f in sorted(df["frameId"].unique())]

    def update(k):
        t = frames[k]
        ax.clear()
        fld = panel(ax, play, df, t, lateral, window, rings)
        if after:
            after(fld, play, t, -1)
        cur = [n for tt, n in notes if tt <= t + 1e-6]
        ax.set_title(("snap" if abs(t) < 0.05 else f"{t:+.1f} s") + (("\n" + cur[-1].replace("\n", " ")) if cur else ""),
                     fontsize=8.2, color=style.INK, loc="left")
        return []

    anim = animation.FuncAnimation(fig, update, frames=range(len(frames)), interval=100)
    html = (anim.to_html5_video(embed_limit=40).replace("<video ", '<video style="max-width:100%;height:auto" ')
            if shutil.which("ffmpeg") else anim.to_jshtml(default_mode="once"))
    plt.close(fig)
    display(HTML(html))


def animation_or_strip(play, moments, lateral, window, rings=(), after=None, ncols=2, width_in=6.2):
    """Video on the website; a numbered, captioned frame strip in the PDF. moments = [(t, tag, note)]."""
    if pdf_build():
        strip([(play, t, tag) for t, tag, _ in moments], lateral, window, notes=[n for *_, n in moments],
              rings=rings, ncols=ncols, width_in=width_in, after=after)
        plt.show()
        return
    video(play, [(t, n) for t, _, n in moments], lateral, window, rings=rings, after=after)


def era_43(off, shell):
    """A 1980s 4-3 Over against a pro set or I (TE to the offense's right), corners 7 off."""
    dfn = [D("WE", "DE", 1.0, T("5", -1), "E"), D("WT", "DT", 1.0, T("1", -1), "T"),
           D("ST", "DT", 1.0, T("3"), "T"), D("SE", "DE", 1.0, T("5") + 0.2, "E"),
           D("SAM", "LB", 4.0, 6.4, "S"), D("MIKE", "LB", 4.5, 0.8, "M"), D("WILL", "LB", 4.5, -3.0, "W"),
           D("LCB", "CB", 6.5, -14.0, "CB"), D("RCB", "CB", 6.5, 14.0, "CB")]
    if shell == "two":
        dfn += [D("FS", "FS", 13.0, -8.0, "FS"), D("SS", "SS", 13.0, 8.0, "SS")]
    else:
        dfn += [D("FS", "FS", 13.0, 0.0, "FS"), D("SS", "SS", 8.0, 7.0, "SS")]
    return dfn


def ghost_off(fld, p, d, w, label="?"):
    x, y = (float(v) for v in _P(fld, p, d, w))
    fld.ax.add_patch(Circle((x, y), 0.75, fc="none", ec=style.OFFENSE, lw=1.3, ls=(0, (2, 1.4)), zorder=8))
    fld.ax.text(x, y, label, ha="center", va="center", fontsize=8, color=style.OFFENSE_DARK, fontweight="bold",
                zorder=9)
```

Put on a game from the early 1970s. The picture looks familiar: two wide receivers, a tight
end, two backs, a quarterback under center. Then watch a receiver run a route. A linebacker hits
him as he leaves the line, a safety hits him again eight yards downfield, and nobody throws a
flag, because none of it is illegal. Watch an offensive tackle pass-block: his fists are balled
against his chest and his elbows are out, like a man shielding himself in a crowd. The league
trimmed that downfield contact twice in the mid-1970s and it made little difference: in 1977 NFL
teams averaged **17.2 points a game**, the fewest since 1942. Twenty-one years later a single
team, the 1998 Minnesota Vikings, scored 556 points, a league record at the time. What happened in
between? The answer starts with two short changes to the rulebook in March 1978, and with the
twenty years of move and counter-move they set off, a story in which every offensive idea you now
see on Sundays met a defensive answer, and every answer started the next round.

**You'll be able to:**

- State the two 1978 rule changes (the Mel Blount rule and open-hand pass blocking), say what
  each one changed on the field, and read the jump they produced in the league's passing numbers.
- Tell Air Coryell from the West Coast offense by what each asks the quarterback to do, say which
  1978 rule each one leaned on, and recognize Gibbs's one-back offense, the run-and-shoot and the
  K-Gun on old film.
- Explain each defensive answer as a response to something specific: nickel and dime to the third
  receiver, Arnsparger's 53 and the 3-4 to the need to disguise a fourth rusher, the 46 to the
  two-back offense, the zone blitz to the quick passing game; and explain why the 3-4 made room for
  a new kind of player, the stand-up pass rusher Lawrence Taylor, and how offenses answered him.
- Explain why the left tackle became the blind-side tackle, and what an offense does about the best
  pass rusher on the field.
- Explain what the 1994 rule package changed (the two-point conversion and kickoffs from the 30),
  do the expected-points arithmetic behind the two-point decision, and say when the score flips it.
- Explain free agency (1993) and the salary cap (1994), and name three ways they changed how teams
  build and coach.

and [chip](../../appendices/glossary.qmd#gl-chip), from
[Pass Protection](../04-the-passing-game/04-02-pass-protection.qmd).

*Reading the diagrams:* offense is blue circles (Q quarterback; R or T the running back, F the
fullback, H a halfback or H-back; X, Y, Z the receivers, Y usually the tight end; on the line, T G
C G T are the tackles, guards and center). Defense is outlined squares (E end, T tackle, N nose,
L or B linebackers, with M, W and S for the Mike, Will and Sam; CB corners; FS and SS safeties).
Solid arrows are routes and runs, dashed orange arrows are defenders' drops and options, a bar at
the end of a line is a block, and the dashed brown line is the pass. A green ring marks the player
to watch. The left-edge numbers give depth in yards past the line of scrimmage.
:::

## Where the story starts: the 1977 problem

[The previous chapter](11-01-single-wing-to-scoring-drought.qmd) ended with the defenses on top,
and the recap is short. Until 1974 a defender could hit a receiver anywhere on the field until the
ball was in the air, and a pass blocker had to keep his hands in to his chest and block with his
forearms and shoulders. The league trimmed downfield contact in 1974, and in 1977 it allowed each
receiver to be contacted only once and banned the head slap that pass rushers like Deacon Jones had
used to stun blockers.[^hof7477] None of it worked. In 1977 teams scored 17.2 points a game; only 40
percent of offensive plays were passes; and 5.7 percent of passes were intercepted, more than one
in eighteen.

Why didn't "only once" fix it? Because the defense chose *where* to spend its one hit. A pass play
is a timed contract: the receiver promises to be at a spot at a moment, and the quarterback throws
to the spot. One collision at 8 yards, from a linebacker the receiver had to run past anyway, was
enough to make him half a second late, and a late receiver on a timed throw means an incompletion
or an interception. The 1977 rule cut the number of hits but left the one that mattered. And for the
pass blockers nothing had changed at all.

The league had reasons to care beyond taste. In October 1977 Pete Rozelle signed television contracts
with all three networks that would carry every regular-season game from 1978, then the largest
television package ever negotiated, and an expanded 16-game schedule was coming with
them.[^hof77tv] A sport selling itself to a national audience every week needed points, and
points in the 1970s came mostly from long, grinding drives that defenses were winning more often
every season.

## Spring 1978: two rules, one direction

In March 1978 the owners passed a package of changes. Two of them did almost all the work.[^rules78]

### The receiver goes free: the Mel Blount rule

The first rule drew a line five yards past the line of scrimmage. Inside that line, a defender
squared up in front of a receiver may still contact him, jamming him, rerouting him, knocking him off
the line, and he may stay on him (the rule's word was *maintain* contact) until the receiver gets
level with him or crosses the five-yard line. It is not a one-hit rule; it is a five-yard zone.
Beyond it, while the quarterback still has the ball, a defender may not initiate contact that
impedes the receiver: no shove, no chuck, no collision. Once the ball is thrown, any contact that
interferes is pass interference, as before. (Today's rulebook adds one condition worth knowing for
old and new film alike: the restriction holds only while the quarterback is in the pocket with the
ball. Once he scrambles out of it, defenders may chuck receivers downfield again; see
[Contact Rules and Penalties](../09-special-teams-and-the-rules-that-shape-strategy/09-03-contact-rules-and-penalties.qmd).) That five-yard zone is the
[**Mel Blount rule (1978)**](../../appendices/glossary.qmd#gl-mel-blount-rule-1978): *a defender may
contact a receiver only within five yards of the line, before the throw.* The name honors, if that
is the word, Pittsburgh's 6-foot-3 cornerback Mel Blount, the 1975 defensive player of the year,
whose bump-and-run coverage was so physical that the league's answer was named after him. Some
accounts attach the nickname to the 1977 one-chuck rule instead; the five-yard rule of 1978 is the
one most people mean.[^blountname]

```{python}
#| label: fig-blount-rule
#| fig-cap: "The 1978 contact rule, on one tight end's seam route (illustrative). Left, before 1978: the Sam (S) hits Y at the line, the Mike (M) knocks him off his path at 8 yards, and the strong safety hits him again at 12, so he arrives late and wide of where his quarterback expects him. Before 1974 all three hits were legal. Under the 1977 one-contact rule only one was, so the defense let Y off the line clean and saved its hit for the Mike at 8 yards (hit 2, outlined), which alone is enough to make him late. Right, from 1978: contact is legal only in the green zone, the first five yards past the line. Past it the Mike and the safety may not touch Y until the ball is thrown, so he runs his seam on time and on his path."
#| code-summary: "Show the Python"
def blount_panel(ax, era):
    off = [p for p in line("short") if p.key in ("C", "RG", "RT")] + [
        O("Y", "TE", -0.7, 4.8, "Y"), O("QB", "QB", -1.9, 0.0, "Q")]
    dfn = [D("SAM", "LB", 1.0, 7.0, "S"), D("MIKE", "LB", 4.5, 2.2, "M"), D("SS", "S", 15.0, 10.4, "SS"),
           D("DT", "DT", 1.0, T("3"), "T"), D("DE", "DE", 1.0, T("5") + 0.3, "E")]
    p = Play(off, dfn, los=35, to_go=None)
    if era == "old":
        go_to(p, "Y", (16.5, 9.6), kind="route", via=[(1.0, 5.3), (2.6, 6.4), (7.6, 5.5), (9.2, 7.6), (12.0, 7.9)])
        go_to(p, "MIKE", (7.4, 4.8), kind="path")
        go_to(p, "SS", (12.8, 8.6), kind="path")
    else:
        go_to(p, "Y", (17.5, 5.1), kind="route", via=[(1.0, 5.3), (2.4, 5.2)])
        go_to(p, "MIKE", (8.5, 3.2), kind="path")
        go_to(p, "SS", (16.5, 7.4), kind="path")
    p.highlight("Y")
    fld = draw(p, ax=ax, lateral=(-3.6, 12.6), window=(-3.4, 19.0), title=False)
    band(fld, p, 0.0, 5.0, -3.6, 12.6, color=GREEN, alpha=0.09 if era == "new" else 0.0,
         lw=0.0 if era == "old" else 0.9)
    if era == "old":
        for (d, w), lab, (td, tw) in [((1.0, 5.3), "hit 1", (2.5, 4.0)), ((7.6, 5.5), "hit 2", (7.2, 2.9)),
                                       ((12.0, 7.9), "hit 3", (11.0, 10.2))]:
            spot(fld, p, d, w, ms=9)
            say(fld, p, td, tw, lab, color=style.DEFENSE_DARK, fontsize=7, weight="bold")
        x2, y2 = _P(fld, p, 7.6, 5.5)
        ax.add_patch(Circle((float(x2), float(y2)), 1.15, fc="none", ec=style.DEFENSE_DARK, lw=1.3, zorder=7.5))
        say(fld, p, 6.0, 9.4, "1977: the one\nlegal hit", color=style.DEFENSE_DARK, fontsize=6.6)
        say(fld, p, 16.6, 3.2, "Y arrives late,\noff his path", color=style.OFFENSE_DARK, fontsize=7)
        title(ax, "Before 1978: hit him downfield\n(any number of times before 1974)")
    else:
        spot(fld, p, 1.0, 5.3, ms=9)
        say(fld, p, 2.5, 4.0, "hit", color=style.DEFENSE_DARK, fontsize=7, weight="bold")
        say(fld, p, 2.6, -0.3, "first 5 yards:\ncontact allowed", color=GREEN, fontsize=6.8)
        say(fld, p, 11.0, 1.2, "past 5 yards:\nhands off until\nthe ball is thrown", color=style.INK_2, fontsize=6.8)
        say(fld, p, 16.6, 1.6, "Y arrives on\ntime, on his path", color=style.OFFENSE_DARK, fontsize=7)
        title(ax, "From 1978: contact only in\nthe first 5 yards")
    ruler(fld, p, depths=(5, 10, 15))
    return fld


fig, axes = plt.subplots(1, 2, figsize=(6.4, 4.9))
blount_panel(axes[0], "old")
blount_panel(axes[1], "new")
fig.tight_layout(w_pad=1.0)
plt.show()
```

@fig-blount-rule shows what changed for the defense. Before, every defender between the receiver
and his landmark was a potential speed bump. A zone defense could *re-route* receivers: knock
crossers off their paths, steer a tight end toward a waiting safety, and destroy the timing a
passing game depends on. After 1978, only the defenders near the line got a shot, and only once the
receiver was past them was he free. A linebacker dropping to 8 yards could no longer hit the tight
end running past him. He had to *cover* him, with his feet, and linebackers built to take on
guards are not built to run with tight ends.

The deepest effect was on **timing**. A route that can be disrupted anywhere can't be thrown on a
count, because the quarterback never knows when his receiver will arrive. A route that can be
disrupted only in the first five yards can be. If the receiver gets a clean release, he will be at
12 yards, breaking toward the sideline, at the same moment on Sunday that he was in Wednesday's
practice. The quarterback can throw to the *spot* before the receiver turns around. Every timing
route you have met in this book, from the [quick game](../04-the-passing-game/04-03-quick-game.qmd)
to the [dropback concepts](../04-the-passing-game/04-04-dropback-concepts.qmd), assumes that.

### The blocker gets his hands: open-hand pass protection

The second rule was about the other end of the play. From 1978 an offensive lineman pass-blocking
could **extend his arms and open his hands**. That sounds like a technicality; it changed the
geometry of the pocket. A blocker restricted to his chest and forearms meets the rusher body to
body, and a rusher who gets his shoulder past the blocker's hip is past him. A blocker who can extend
his arms meets the rusher at arm's length and can *steer* him: feel which way
he is going and push him further that way, past the quarterback, while staying between him and
the passer. That is the [punch](../../appendices/glossary.qmd#gl-punch) of
[Pass Protection](../04-the-passing-game/04-02-pass-protection.qmd), and it doesn't exist without
the 1978 rule. Holding (grabbing and restricting the rusher) stayed illegal. What changed is that a
lineman could now meet the rusher with extended arms and open hands instead of his chest and
forearms.

More time in the pocket matters most to the throws that take the longest. A three-step drop and a
quick slant need little protection; a seven-step drop and a 20-yard post need a lot. So the second
rule pointed the same way as the first: toward the deep and intermediate passing game the 1970s
defenses had strangled.

::: {.callout-important title="Why it exists"}
The two rules attacked the 1970s defensive advantage from both ends at once. The Blount rule took
away the defense's best way to wreck a route (hitting the receiver), and the hands rule took away
its best way to wreck the quarterback's clock (beating a blocker who couldn't use his arms). The
league's stated aim, in the Hall of Fame's words, was to "open up the game." What the
rules gave up was a style of defense. A team built on big, physical defensive backs who won by
contact, like the Steelers who gave the rule its name, now had to win with speed and position
instead. And the Steelers are the first example of the chapter's theme, that the team that adapts
first wins: Pittsburgh won the next two Super Bowls with a passing game. Terry Bradshaw was the
league's MVP in 1978 and threw for 318 yards and four touchdowns in the 35–31 win over Dallas in
Super Bowl XIII.[^openup]
:::

### And the rest of the package

Three smaller changes rode along, and each fits the same story. The schedule grew from 14 games to
16 and a second wild card was added in each conference, which meant more games to televise. The
league added a **seventh official**, the side judge, partly to rule on what happens downfield: a
new contact rule needs someone standing where the contact happens. And the next spring, in 1979,
officials were told to blow the whistle as soon as a quarterback was "clearly in the grasp" of a
tackler, the first of many rules protecting the passer that the league's investment in passing
would require.[^grasp]

::: {.callout-caution title="Common misconception"}
"The Mel Blount rule outlawed bump-and-run coverage." It didn't. Inside five yards a cornerback can
still jam a receiver at the line, and teams have played press coverage ever since, from the 1980s
Raiders to Seattle's press Cover 3 of the 2010s. What the rule removed was the *second*, third and
fourth hit downfield, the ones that let a zone defense steer receivers wherever it wanted. It was
also not the last word. Officials let a good deal of downfield contact go in the years that
followed, the league renewed its emphasis on the rule in its 1994 package (later in this chapter),
and it was called strictly only from 2004, the "Ty Law rule" of
[Coverage Fundamentals](../06-pass-coverage/06-01-coverage-fundamentals.qmd). On old film, expect to
see more contact past five yards than the rulebook allowed.
:::

::: {.callout-note title="Madden vs. real life"}
In a video game the rulebook is fixed, and the best plays are the best plays forever. In the NFL
the rulebook is rewritten every spring, and schemes chase the rewrites. The 1978 changes are the
clearest example in the sport's history: no coach invented a play that ended the 1970s scoring
drought. The owners did, by changing what a defender was allowed to do with his hands, and then
the coaches spent twenty years finding out what that made possible. When a rule changes, ask the
question this chapter asks over and over: *what did this take away, and from whom?*
:::

## What the numbers did

How big was the change? Season-level league totals answer that. Pro Football Reference keeps a
year-by-year table of league averages, and @fig-league-trend draws four of its rates for every
season from 1970 to 1999.[^pfr] Rates matter here, not totals, because the schedule grew from 14 to
16 games in 1978 and two seasons (1982 and 1987) were cut short by strikes.

```{python}
#| label: fig-league-trend
#| fig-cap: "The NFL's passing game, 1970 to 1999: four league-wide rates by season, from Pro Football Reference's league averages. The shaded years are before the 1978 rules (dashed line); the dotted line marks the 1994 rule package. Passes as a share of plays jumped from 40% in 1977 to 49% in 1980 and kept rising. Interceptions per 100 passes fell from 5.7 to 3.4 over twenty years. Net yards per pass attempt rose from 5.2 to 6.0 and then stopped. Scoring rose from 17.2 points to the low 20s, sagged in the early 1990s and rose again after 1994."
#| code-summary: "Show the Python (league averages, 1970-1999)"
# Pro Football Reference, "NFL League Year-by-Year Averages" (per team per game, and season totals).
LEAGUE = pd.read_csv(io.StringIO("""season,ppg,nya,att,cmp,int,td,rush_att

L = LEAGUE.assign(pass_share=100 * LEAGUE.att / (LEAGUE.att + LEAGUE.rush_att),
                  cmp_pct=100 * LEAGUE.cmp / LEAGUE.att, int_pct=100 * LEAGUE.int / LEAGUE.att)

fig, axes = plt.subplots(2, 2, figsize=(6.5, 5.2), sharex=True)
panels = [
    (axes[0, 0], "ppg", "Points per team per game", "{:.1f}", (15.5, 23), {1977: "below", 1983: "above", 1993: "below", 1999: "above"}),
    (axes[0, 1], "pass_share", "Passes as a share of plays (%)", "{:.0f}%", (36, 59), {1977: "below", 1981: "above", 1999: "above"}),
    (axes[1, 0], "int_pct", "Interceptions per 100 passes", "{:.1f}", (2.5, 6.5), {1977: "above", 1999: "below"}),

for ax, col, ttl, fmt, ylim, labs in panels:
    ax.axvspan(1969.5, 1977.5, color=style.GRID, alpha=0.45, lw=0, zorder=0)
    ax.axvline(1978, color=style.INK_2, lw=0.9, ls=(0, (3, 2)), zorder=1)
```
