```{python}
                    color=style.INK, ha=ha, va="center", zorder=4,
                    bbox=dict(boxstyle="round,pad=0.1", fc=style.SURFACE, ec="none", alpha=0.85))
    ax.set_title(ttl, fontsize=8.8)
    ax.set_ylim(*ylim)
    ax.set_xlim(1969.5, 2002.3)
    ax.tick_params(labelsize=7)
    ax.grid(axis="x", visible=False)
for ax in axes.flat:
    lo, hi = ax.get_ylim()
    ax.text(1973.5, hi - 0.03 * (hi - lo), "before\n1978", fontsize=6.6, color=style.INK_2, ha="center", va="top")
for ax in axes[0]:
    lo, hi = ax.get_ylim()
    ax.text(1978.4, lo + 0.02 * (hi - lo), "1978 rules", fontsize=6.6, color=style.INK_2, ha="left", va="bottom")
    ax.text(1994.4, lo + 0.02 * (hi - lo), "1994\npackage", fontsize=6.6, color=style.MUTED, ha="left", va="bottom")
for ax in axes[1]:
    ax.set_xticks([1970, 1978, 1986, 1994, 1999])
fig.tight_layout(h_pad=1.2, w_pad=1.6)
plt.show()
```

Read @fig-league-trend panel by panel.

- **Passes as a share of plays** (top right) is the cleanest signal, and the biggest. In 1977 teams
  threw on 40 percent of their plays. By 1980 it was 49 percent, and after 1983 it never went below
  half again. Offenses decided, almost at once, that throwing had become a better deal.
- **Interceptions** (bottom left) fell from 5.7 per 100 passes in 1977 to 4.6 in 1979 and 1980,
  and kept falling for twenty years, to 3.4 in 1999. A receiver who can't be knocked off his route
  is where the quarterback expects him to be, and a ball thrown to the right spot is harder to
  intercept. Completion rate rose too, from 51 percent in 1977 to 56 percent in 1980.
- **Net yards per pass attempt** (bottom right: passing yards minus sack yardage, divided by
  attempts plus sacks) jumped from 5.2 in 1977 to 6.0 in 1980 and then stopped. Through the 1980s
  and 1990s it wandered between 5.7 and 6.1. Each throw got a little better, once, and then the
  defenses caught up with it.
- **Points** (top left) went from 17.2 to 20.5 in three seasons. Note 1978 itself: only 18.3. The
  rules arrived that season, but the offenses that exploited them took a year or two to arrive.

The pattern in those last two panels is the theme of this chapter. A rule change opens a gap, the
offense pours into it, and then the defense adapts and the efficiency gain levels off. What stays
is the *volume*: teams kept throwing more, because once the defense adjusted to stop the pass,
it had less left over to stop the run. And at the far right of the points panel is the next round of
the same cycle: scoring sagged to 18.7 in 1992 and 1993, and the league changed the rules again
(the 1994 package, later in this chapter).

Averages show the floor of the new game, not its ceiling. The best offenses ran far ahead of the
league line: in 1984 Dan Marino threw for 5,084 yards, and in 1998 the Vikings scored 556 points,
34.8 a game against a league average of 21.3. Both were records at the time.

## Offense's first answer: Air Coryell stretches the field deep

The coach most ready for 1978 was already in the league. **Don Coryell** had built pass-first
offenses at San Diego State in the 1960s and with the St. Louis Cardinals from 1973, and on
September 25, 1978, four games into the season, he took over the San Diego Chargers. Coryell's offense, built on Sid Gillman's idea that a
defense should be made to cover every blade of grass, put receivers in motion, lined them up all
over the formation, and made the deep throw the first option on most passing plays. His
quarterback, **Dan Fouts**, had spent five unremarkable seasons in San Diego. In 1979 he threw for
4,082 yards, breaking Joe Namath's single-season record of 4,007; in 1981 he threw for 4,802, and he
became the first quarterback to pass for 4,000 yards in three straight seasons. The 1979 Chargers
were the first AFC West champion to call more passes than runs, and San Diego led the league in
passing yards every season from 1978 to 1983.[^coryell]

The offense needed a different kind of tight end, and Coryell had one. **Kellen Winslow**, a
first-round pick in 1979, was big enough to line up next to the tackle and fast enough to run with
safeties. Coryell split him out, put him in motion, and threw to him down the seams. A tight end
who can't be hit past five yards and can outrun a linebacker is exactly the matchup the new rules
created.

```{python}
#| label: fig-coryell
#| fig-cap: "Air Coryell: '896' from a two-back I formation against Cover 2 (illustrative). In the digit system X runs an 8 (a post), Y, the tight end (ringed), a 9 (a go, up the seam), and Z a 6 (a dig at 15 yards). Both backs and the line stay in to block, seven blockers, while the quarterback takes a seven-step drop. The ball goes to Y in the seam between the two deep safeties, each responsible for half the field. The linebackers drop to about 10 yards and the corners squat in the flats, and none of them may touch a receiver once he is five yards past the line."
#| code-summary: "Show the Python"
# ------------------------------------------------------------- Air Coryell: 896 against Cover 2
off = line("short") + [O("QB", "QB", -1.9, 0.0, "Q"), O("FB", "FB", -4.5, 0.0, "F"), O("RB", "RB", -7.0, 0.0, "R"),
                       O("Y", "TE", -0.7, 4.8, "Y"), O("X", "WR", -0.7, -14.0, "X"), O("Z", "WR", -1.5, 14.0, "Z")]
p = Play(off, era_43(off, "two"), los=30, to_go=None)
p.route("X", r.post(stem=10))
p.route("Y", r.seam(22))
p.route("Z", r.dig(depth=15, width=13))
p.dropback(7.0)
p.drop("FS", (19.0, -9.0), zone=(9, 16), label="deep half")
p.drop("SS", (19.0, 9.0), zone=(9, 16), label="deep half")
for k in ("SAM", "MIKE", "WILL"):
    q = p.players[k]
    p.drop(k, (10.0, q.w * 1.6 if k != "MIKE" else 1.0))
for k in ("LCB", "RCB"):
    q = p.players[k]
    p.drop(k, (5.0, q.w * 1.02))
for k in ("LT", "LG", "C", "RG", "RT"):
    p.block(k, pts=[(-1.2, 0.0)])
p.block("FB", pts=[(0.2, -2.0)])
p.block("RB", pts=[(1.6, 2.6)])
p.pass_to("Y", t=2.75)
p.highlight("Y")
fld = draw(p, width_in=5.6, lateral=(-18.5, 18.5), window=(-10.5, 25.5), title=False)
ruler(fld, p, depths=(5, 10, 15, 20))
say(fld, p, -8.4, 3.6, "7-step drop", fontsize=7)
say(fld, p, 22.6, -2.7, "X: 8 (post)", color=style.OFFENSE_DARK, fontsize=7, weight="bold")
say(fld, p, 22.4, 7.2, "Y: 9 (go)", color=style.OFFENSE_DARK, fontsize=7, weight="bold")
say(fld, p, 16.4, 12.6, "Z: 6 (dig)", color=style.OFFENSE_DARK, fontsize=7, weight="bold")
say(fld, p, -5.6, -11.0, "seven block:\nline + both backs", fontsize=6.8)
plt.show()
```

@fig-coryell is a Coryell-style call in the digit system of
[Offensive Systems](../04-the-passing-game/04-08-offensive-systems-and-languages.qmd): "896" gives X
an 8 (a post), Y a 9 (a go, here up the seam), and Z a 6 (a dig). Three receivers attack three
spots deep, and against the two deep safeties of [Cover 2](../../appendices/glossary.qmd#gl-cover-2)
the tight end's seam splits them. Notice what pays for it: both backs stay in to block, seven
blockers for a seven-step drop, so the quarterback has time to let the deep routes develop.

**Why it works, and what it costs.** Air Coryell answers the 1978 rules with *depth*. Receivers who
can't be rerouted can be sent long, and blockers who can use their hands can hold up long enough for
them to get there. The cost is everything a deep passing game always costs: long drops, longer
protection, fewer receivers in routes, and interceptions when the throw is late. Coryell's Chargers
had famously poor defenses and never reached a Super Bowl. His ideas lasted anyway. They ran through
his assistants (Joe Gibbs, Ernie Zampese) to Norv Turner's Dallas offenses of the 1990s and to
Mike Martz's 1999 St. Louis Rams, the "Greatest Show on Turf."

::: {.callout-note title="Film room: San Diego Chargers 1981 — the Epic in Miami"}
**The game:** the AFC divisional playoff at the Miami Orange Bowl on January 2, 1982. San Diego led
24–0 in the first quarter, Miami came back to lead, and the Chargers won 41–38 in overtime. Fouts
completed 33 of 53 passes for 433 yards, all NFL playoff records at the time; Winslow caught 13
passes, also a playoff record, for 166 yards, and blocked a field goal at the end of regulation that
would have won it for Miami. Both teams finished exhausted in the Florida heat, and the game is
still ranked among the best ever played.[^epic]

**What to notice:** the Chargers' receivers lining up anywhere (Winslow wide, in the slot, in
motion), the depth of the routes, and how often the first read is downfield. Then notice the
defenses: both teams were playing the 1970s way, with a safety and linebackers waiting to collide
with receivers, and on almost every throw nobody is allowed to.
:::

## Offense's second answer: Walsh stretches it sideways

Bill Walsh read the same rules the other way. Walsh had built a short passing game in Cincinnati in
the early 1970s, as an assistant to Paul Brown, around a quarterback who couldn't throw deep (the
story is in [Passing Fundamentals](../04-the-passing-game/04-01-passing-fundamentals.qmd)). In
January 1979 the San Francisco 49ers, 2–14 in 1978, made him their head coach. They went 2–14 again in
his first season, but in the third round of the 1979 draft he had taken a Notre Dame quarterback,
Joe Montana. Three seasons later the 49ers beat Cincinnati 26–21 in Super Bowl XVI.[^walsh]

```{python}
#| label: fig-walsh
#| fig-cap: "The West Coast idea: a quick slant with a flat route behind it, from the pro set, against Cover 3 (illustrative). The quarterback takes a three-step drop and throws in about a second. X runs the slant, the halfback (H) runs to the flat, and the tight end (Y) crosses underneath; the fullback (F) and the line block. The Will linebacker (W, ringed) can't cover both the slant and the flat, so he widens for the flat and the ball goes to X (ringed) on the slant, inside him and in front of the corner, who has bailed to his deep third. The thick arrow is X's run after the catch."
#| code-summary: "Show the Python"
# ------------------------------------------------------------- West Coast: slant-flat with a shallow cross
off = line("short") + [O("QB", "QB", -1.9, 0.0, "Q"), O("HB", "RB", -5.0, -2.2, "H"), O("FB", "FB", -5.0, 2.2, "F"),
                       O("Y", "TE", -0.7, 4.8, "Y"), O("X", "WR", -0.7, -13.0, "X"), O("Z", "WR", -1.5, 13.0, "Z")]
p = Play(off, era_43(off, "one"), los=30, to_go=None)
p.dropback(3.2)
p.route("X", [(0, 0), (1.5, 0), (6.2, -4.5)], speed=5.0)
p.run("X", [(4.2, 3.6)])
p.route("HB", [(0, 0), (2.5, 3.5), (6.0, 9.0)], side=-1)
p.route("Y", [(0, 0), (2.5, -1.0), (3.5, -10.0)])
p.route("Z", r.curl(12))
for k in ("LT", "LG", "C", "RG", "RT"):
    p.block(k, pts=[(-1.0, 0.0)])
p.drop("LCB", (11.5, -14.2))
p.drop("WILL", (3.0, -11.0))
p.drop("MIKE", (8.0, 1.0))
p.pass_to("X", t=0.8)
p.highlight("X", "WILL")
fld = draw(p, width_in=6.0, lateral=(-18.5, 16.5), window=(-7.5, 16.5), title=False)
ruler(fld, p, depths=(5, 10, 15))
say(fld, p, 11.1, -1.2, "run after the catch", color=style.OFFENSE_DARK, fontsize=7)
say(fld, p, 3.0, -14.9, "slant", color=style.OFFENSE_DARK, fontsize=7, weight="bold")
say(fld, p, 13.6, -10.6, "W can't cover\nslant and flat", color=style.DEFENSE_DARK, fontsize=7)
say(fld, p, -5.9, 5.6, "3-step drop:\nball out in ~1 s", fontsize=6.8)
plt.show()
```

Walsh's offense treats the short pass as a run. @fig-walsh is the idea in its plainest form: a
three-step drop, and the ball out in about a second to X on a quick slant, while the halfback runs to
the flat behind him and the tight end crosses underneath. The Will linebacker can't cover both the
slant and the flat, a [horizontal stretch](../../appendices/glossary.qmd#gl-horizontal-stretch),
so whichever he chooses, the quarterback throws the other. The receiver catches the ball in stride,
already running, and the yards come after the catch.

**Why the 1978 rules made it work.** Every route in @fig-walsh crosses a defender's face within a
few yards of the line, exactly where re-routing used to wreck them. After 1978, once the receiver
was five yards downfield, the linebacker in his path could do nothing but try to beat him to the
spot, and on a timed throw he never will. Walsh's offense is the timing game at its purest: drops
matched to route depths, the ball thrown to the spot before the receiver turns, and a progression
the quarterback can run in a second and a half. It needs less protection than Coryell's, throws fewer
interceptions, and turns a 5-yard completion into a 15-yard gain. The cost is that it needs an
extremely accurate quarterback and receivers who run every route to the inch, and that it is long and
hard to learn: the West Coast play calls you met in [Offensive Systems](../04-the-passing-game/04-08-offensive-systems-and-languages.qmd)
spell out every receiver's job because the timing has no slack.

Walsh's 49ers won Super Bowls after the 1981, 1984 and 1988 seasons, and his assistants carried
the system everywhere (the coaching tree is in
[Case Study: Bill Walsh's 49ers and the West Coast Offense](../12-case-studies/12-01-walsh-49ers-west-coast.qmd)).
Between them, Coryell and Walsh defined the two ways to pass after 1978: stretch the defense
vertically, or stretch it horizontally. Nearly every passing game since mixes the two.

## Defense's first answer: more defensive backs

Defenses answered the new passing game first with **personnel**. If offenses were going to throw on
half their plays, and to put a third receiver on the field to do it, then a linebacker covering
that third receiver was a losing matchup on half the snaps. The fix was to take a linebacker off and
put a fifth defensive back on: the [nickel](../../appendices/glossary.qmd#gl-nickel). The idea was
older than 1978 (it is usually traced to Philadelphia assistant Jerry Williams around 1960, named by
George Allen, and popularized by Don Shula and Bill Arnsparger's Miami Dolphins in the
1970s),[^nickel] but after 1978 it went from a special package to an everyday one. In long-yardage
situations defenses went further, to the [dime](../../appendices/glossary.qmd#gl-dime): six
defensive backs.

Each substitution is a trade. A nickel defense has one fewer player built to take on blockers, so
it is softer against the run. And substitution became a game of its own: offenses changed their
personnel to draw a defense into the wrong package, the
[substitution matching](../../appendices/glossary.qmd#gl-substitution-matching) of
[Personnel Groupings](../02-personnel-and-formations/02-01-personnel-groupings.qmd). A defense in
nickel against two tight ends is too light; a defense in base against three receivers is too slow.
Hold on to that trade; it decides the K-Gun story later in this chapter.

## Defense's second answer: Arnsparger's 53 and the 3-4

The second answer was about the *front*, and it had started in Miami before 1978.
**Bill Arnsparger**, Don Shula's defensive coordinator, asked the Dolphins to trade for a Cleveland
linebacker named **Bob Matheson** before the 1971 season, and built a package around him. Matheson
lined up at the end of the line on the tight end's side, standing up. On some snaps he rushed the
passer like a defensive end; on others he dropped into coverage like a linebacker. The package was
named for his jersey number: the [**53 defense**](../../appendices/glossary.qmd#gl-53-defense),
*Arnsparger's front in which one hybrid player decided, snap by snap, whether the defense was a 4-3
or a 3-4.* The package dates from the start of the 1972 season, and the 1972 Dolphins, Arnsparger's "No-Name
Defense," went 17–0.[^matheson]

```{python}
#| label: fig-53
#| fig-cap: "Arnsparger's 53 (illustrative, against a 1970s pro set). Three linemen have a hand down; Bob Matheson, number 53 (ringed), stands at the end of the line outside the tight end. At the snap he either rushes, making a four-man line (a 4-3 look), or drops into coverage, making four linebackers (a 3-4 look). The blockers have to decide before the snap whether to account for him, and they can't know which he will do."
#| code-summary: "Show the Python"
# ------------------------------------------------------------------ the 53
off = line("short") + [O("QB", "QB", -1.9, 0.0, "Q"), O("HB", "RB", -5.0, -2.2, "H"), O("FB", "FB", -5.0, 2.2, "F"),
                       O("Y", "TE", -0.7, 4.8, "Y"), O("X", "WR", -0.7, -13.0, "X"), O("Z", "WR", -1.5, 13.0, "Z")]
dfn = [D("WE", "DE", 1.0, T("5", -1), "E"), D("NT", "NT", 1.0, 0.0, "N"), D("SE", "DE", 1.0, T("5"), "E"),
       D("M53", "LB", 1.2, T("9") + 0.4, "53"), D("WLB", "LB", 1.6, -6.6, "L"),
       D("ILB1", "LB", 4.5, -2.0, "L"), D("ILB2", "LB", 4.5, 2.0, "L"),
       D("LCB", "CB", 7.0, -13.0, "CB"), D("RCB", "CB", 7.0, 13.0, "CB"),
       D("FS", "FS", 12.5, -3.0, "FS"), D("SS", "SS", 9.0, 8.0, "SS")]
p = Play(off, dfn, los=35, to_go=None)
p.highlight("M53")
fld = draw(p, width_in=6.2, lateral=(-16.5, 16.5), window=(-7.5, 14.5), title=False)
dashed(fld, p, [(1.2, 6.2), (-1.6, 6.9), (-4.4, 3.4)], color=style.DEFENSE_DARK, lw=1.6, dash="-")
dashed(fld, p, [(1.2, 6.2), (4.5, 7.6), (7.6, 9.6)], color=style.DEFENSE_DARK, lw=1.6)
say(fld, p, -4.2, 9.4, "rush: a fourth\nlineman (a 4-3)", color=style.DEFENSE_DARK, fontsize=7.2)
say(fld, p, 10.8, 2.6, "or drop: a fourth\nlinebacker (a 3-4)", color=style.DEFENSE_DARK, fontsize=7.2)
say(fld, p, 3.2, -9.6, "three linemen\nwith hands down", fontsize=7)
point_to(fld, p, (3.0, -6.9), (1.0, -4.0), "", fontsize=1, shrink=6)
plt.show()
```

Look at @fig-53 from the quarterback's side. Before the snap there are three linemen with a hand on
the ground and a fourth man standing at the end of the line. Is it four rushers or three? The
quarterback and his blockers have to decide where Matheson is going before he goes, and they
have no way to know. If they block him and he drops, a blocker is wasted and a linebacker is
covering a receiver they thought was open. If they ignore him and he rushes, he is a free rusher.
Arnsparger's own phrase for what the 53 gave him, in a later interview, was the ability to "rush
five guys and cover with six" from a look that showed neither. He called it "safe pressure," and
it is the seed of the zone blitz.

The rest of the league took the alignment more than the trick. Through the mid-1970s, teams that had
learned the Oklahoma 5-2 in college stood up its ends and called it a 3-4 (the competing origin
claims are laid out in [Odd and Hybrid Fronts](../05-defensive-fronts-and-run-defense/05-03-odd-and-hybrid-fronts.qmd)),
and by the late 1970s and early 1980s it was the league's most common base defense. The 3-4
fitted the post-1978 game for a reason that had nothing to do with the nose tackle: its outside
linebackers stand up at the end of the line, where they can rush or drop, so a 3-4 is a 53 on every
snap. The offense never knows for certain which of the two edge players is coming. And it creates a
place on the field for a particular kind of athlete, a linebacker who is really a pass rusher,
the [stand-up edge](../../appendices/glossary.qmd#gl-stand-up-edge). In 1981 the most famous one
of all arrived.

## Lawrence Taylor and the blind side

The New York Giants took **Lawrence Taylor** from North Carolina with the second pick of the 1981
draft and played him at outside linebacker in their 3-4. He was the league's defensive player of the
year as a rookie, again in 1982, and a third time in 1986, when he had 20.5 sacks and became the
first defensive player voted the league's MVP unanimously. Bill Parcells, his defensive
coordinator and then head coach, and Bill Belichick, the Giants' defensive coordinator from 1985,
built the defense around the fact that no one could block him.[^lt]

Taylor's speed broke the way offenses protected the passer. Through the 1970s, a blitzing
linebacker was a running back's problem: the back stayed in to block whichever linebacker came. A
running back blocking Lawrence Taylor was a mismatch, and teams spent the 1980s inventing better
answers. San Francisco's Walsh, in a January 1982 playoff game against the Giants, assigned his best blocker,
guard John Ayers, to him, which other teams copied; then coaches moved the job to the tackle, and in the end to
whole protection schemes built around where Taylor was (the slide, the chip and the help side of
[Pass Protection](../04-the-passing-game/04-02-pass-protection.qmd)).

Where Taylor lined up mattered as much as how fast he was. He rushed most often from the defense's
right side, the offense's left (he was the Giants' right
outside linebacker), and that is where a right-handed quarterback is most exposed.

```{python}
#| label: fig-blind-side
#| fig-cap: "Why the left tackle matters (illustrative). A right-handed quarterback at the top of his drop. As he sets to throw, his left shoulder points downfield and his eyes go with it, so he can see the area shaded green but not the area shaded orange, behind his left shoulder. The edge rusher on the right (the defense's left) comes at him where he can see and avoid him. The one on the left (ringed) comes from the blind side, and if he beats the left tackle (ringed) around the edge, he arrives unseen. Defenses put their best pass rusher on that side, so offenses put their best pass blocker there to meet him."
#| code-summary: "Show the Python"
# ------------------------------------------------------------------ the blind side
off = line("short") + [O("QB", "QB", -7.5, 0.0, "Q"), O("Y", "TE", -0.7, 4.8, "Y")]
dfn = [D("LE", "OLB", 1.0, -6.8, "E"), D("LDT", "DT", 1.0, T("3", -1), "T"), D("RDT", "DT", 1.0, T("3"), "T"),
       D("RE", "DE", 1.0, T("9") + 0.4, "E")]
p = Play(off, dfn, los=35, to_go=None)
go_to(p, "LE", (-6.6, -2.4), kind="rush", via=[(-2.4, -7.6), (-5.6, -5.2)])
go_to(p, "RE", (-5.4, 3.0), kind="rush", via=[(-2.4, 7.2), (-4.8, 5.4)], speed=4.0)
go_to(p, "LT", (-3.4, -5.0), kind="block", via=[(-1.6, -4.0)])
go_to(p, "RT", (-2.8, 4.9), kind="block", via=[(-1.4, 3.8)])
for k in ("LG", "C", "RG"):
    p.block(k, pts=[(-1.0, 0.0)])
p.block("Y", pts=[(-0.4, 0.8)])
p.highlight("LT", "LE")
fld = draw(p, width_in=6.0, lateral=(-13.5, 13.5), window=(-13.5, 6.5), title=False)
qx, qy = (float(v) for v in _P(fld, p, -7.5, 0.0))
fld.ax.add_patch(Wedge((qx, qy), 9.0, -35, 140, fc=style.THIRD, alpha=0.12, ec=style.THIRD, lw=0.8, zorder=1))
fld.ax.add_patch(Wedge((qx, qy), 6.0, 150, 285, fc=style.DEFENSE, alpha=0.13, ec=style.DEFENSE, lw=0.8,
                       ls=(0, (3, 2)), zorder=1))
say(fld, p, 3.6, 8.4, "what he sees\nas he sets to throw", color=GREEN, fontsize=7)
say(fld, p, -11.6, -5.0, "his blind side:\nbehind his left shoulder", color=style.DEFENSE_DARK, fontsize=7)
say(fld, p, 4.0, -7.4, "the most dangerous rusher\nlines up over here", color=style.DEFENSE_DARK, fontsize=7)
point_to(fld, p, (-3.2, -10.6), (-0.7, -3.2), "left tackle", color=style.OFFENSE_DARK, fontsize=7.2, shrink=9)
say(fld, p, -9.6, 3.6, "right-handed QB\nat the top of his drop", color=style.INK_2, fontsize=6.8)
plt.show()
```

@fig-blind-side shows why. A right-handed quarterback dropping back from under center turns his
body to the right as he drops, and when he sets to throw, his left shoulder points at his target and
his eyes go downfield. Everything coming from behind his left shoulder is outside his field of view.
A rusher from the right side is in front of him or at the edge of his vision, and he can step up or
slide away from it. A rusher from the left arrives unseen, at full speed, at a quarterback holding
the ball away from his body. That produces fumbles and injuries. Lawrence Taylor's sack of
Washington's Joe Theismann on *Monday Night Football* in November 1985, which broke Theismann's leg
and ended his career, came from that side (the scene opens Michael Lewis's book *The Blind Side*;
see [The Twenty-Two](../01-foundations/01-03-the-twenty-two.qmd)).

The result was a new idea of the offensive line. The
[**blind-side tackle**](../../appendices/glossary.qmd#gl-blind-side-tackle) is *the tackle who protects
the side the quarterback can't see: the left tackle for a right-handed passer*. Teams began to put their best pass
blocker there, to draft him early and, once a salary cap made every dollar a choice (later in this
chapter), to pay him like it. Two caveats keep the idea honest. For a left-handed quarterback
(Steve Young in San Francisco, Mark Brunell in Jacksonville in the 1990s) the blind side is the
right. And the side matters less once defenses learned to move their best rusher around, as they all
do now, and once quarterbacks played from the shotgun and turned less on the drop; today the
right tackle is paid almost as well. The blind side still pulls: when a team has to choose, its
best pass protector usually plays on the left.

## Gibbs: one back, two tight ends, and the counter trey

Taylor's division rival had the most direct answer. **Joe Gibbs**, Coryell's former offensive
coordinator in San Diego, became Washington's head coach in 1981 and played the Giants twice a
year. Gibbs's solution, in his own words, was a game plan built for one man: "We had to try in some
way have a special game plan just for Lawrence Taylor... he's one person that we learned the lesson
the hard way. We lost ball games."[^hback] He took the second back out of the backfield and put
him beside the tackle as an extra blocker. Playbooks of the time labelled the backs Q, H and F, so the
new player kept his letter: the **H-back**, a tight end or fullback who lines up a step off the line,
outside the tackle, where he can block an edge rusher, chip him and release into a route, or go in
motion to the other side. With a second tight end on the line, the formation became the one-back,
two-tight-end set (12 personnel) that Washington made its base: the
[ace](../../appendices/glossary.qmd#gl-ace-formation) of
[Classic Formations](../02-personnel-and-formations/02-03-classic-formations.qmd).

The one-back formation answered more than Taylor. With one back, the defense couldn't key a
fullback to find the run. With two tight ends and an H-back, the offense had extra blockers at the
line who could also go out for passes, so the same formation threatened both. And it fitted the run
game Washington built behind its huge offensive line, the "Hogs": the
[counter trey](../../appendices/glossary.qmd#gl-counter-trey), the guard-and-tackle counter of
[Gap Schemes](../03-the-run-game/03-03-gap-and-power-runs.qmd), in which the back steps one way and
two backside linemen pull the other way to lead him. The language of those runs, and Washington's
"70 Chip" on fourth-and-1 in Super Bowl XVII, are in
[The Language of the Run Game](../03-the-run-game/03-01-run-game-language.qmd).

Gibbs won three Super Bowls, after the 1982, 1987 and 1991 seasons, with three different starting quarterbacks (Joe
Theismann, Doug Williams and Mark Rypien), which says something about how much of the offense was
the system.

## Buddy Ryan's 46, and how the one-back attacked it

While Gibbs was building his offense, Chicago's defensive coordinator **Buddy Ryan** was building
the defense meant to destroy offenses like it. The 46 put eight men near the line, covered the
center and both guards with a nose and two 3-techniques (the bear front), stacked both outside
linebackers on the tight end's side, and usually played man coverage behind a blitz. It
was designed against the two-back offenses of the early 1980s, and against them it was devastating:
the 1985 Bears allowed the fewest points in the league and beat New England 46–10 in Super Bowl XX
(the full plate and Ryan's story are in [Even Fronts](../05-defensive-fronts-and-run-defense/05-02-even-fronts.qmd)).[^46]

The 46's strength was its aggression and its alignment rules: both outside linebackers go to the
tight end. Against a one-back team with two tight ends, the rule becomes a question: *which* tight
end? Whichever side the defense chooses, the other side has fewer defenders, and a counter run pulls
two extra blockers to exactly that side.

Follow @fig-46-counter. The defense sets its stack to the in-line tight end, Y, on the right: two
outside linebackers (W and S) out there, plus the Mike over the right tackle. On the left the
offense faces only the end, a tackle, the nose and the strong safety (SS), who in the 46 plays like
a linebacker. The H-back lines up on that side. At the snap the back jabs right, toward the stack,
and the Mike, reading him, steps that way too. Then the right guard and right tackle pull left. Count
the left side now: the guard kicks out the end, the left tackle and left guard block down on the
tackle and the nose, the H-back takes the safety, and the pulling tackle leads through the hole onto
the Mike. Five blockers for five defenders, and the back has a hole. The two linebackers stacked on
the tight end, the players who make the 46 so dangerous against plays toward them, are chasing from
the wrong side of the field.

Notice what the offense gives up to do this. The center has to block back on the 3-technique the
right guard leaves, the hardest block on the play, and the play only works if the defense commits to
one side. The 46 had answers of its own: it could set its stack to the H-back, or flip it when he
went in motion, or blitz the side the counter was headed for. That is the pattern of this whole
era. The offense found a formation that forced the defense to declare, and the defense found a way
to declare late.

```{python}
#| label: fig-46-counter
#| fig-cap: "The counter trey from a one-back, two-tight-end set against the 46 (simulated, BDB-format tracking; illustrative, not a specific play). The 46 sets both outside linebackers (W, S) and the Mike to the in-line tight end, Y, on the right. 1: left of the ball are only the end, a 3-technique, the nose and the strong safety, with the H-back lined up across from them. 2: the back (green ring) jabs right toward the stack and the Mike steps with him, while the right guard and right tackle (purple rings) pull left. 3: the guard kicks out the end, the left tackle and guard block down, the H-back takes the safety, and the center blocks back on the 3-technique the guard left. 4: the pulling tackle leads onto the Mike; the back is through the hole with only the free safety ahead and the stacked linebackers chasing from the far side. Faint lines are each player's path so far."
#| code-summary: "Show the Python (simulated play, video on the web, frame strip in print)"
def one_back_vs_46():
    """Gibbs-style one-back (12 personnel: Y in-line right, H-back off the left tackle) against the 46,
    which sets its two outside linebackers to the in-line tight end. Counter trey (GT counter) left."""
    off = line("short") + [O("QB", "QB", -1.9, 0.0, "Q"), O("RB", "RB", -7.0, 0.0, "R"),
                           O("Y", "TE", -0.7, 4.8, "Y"), O("H", "TE", -1.5, -4.6, "H"),
                           O("X", "WR", -0.7, -14.0, "X"), O("Z", "WR", -1.5, 13.0, "Z")]
    bear = [D("WE", "DE", 1.0, -(3.2 + 1.5), "E"), D("WT", "DT", 1.0, T("3", -1), "T"), D("NT", "NT", 1.0, 0.0, "N"),
            D("ST", "DT", 1.0, T("3", 1), "T"), D("WILL", "LB", 1.3, 4.1, "W"), D("SAM", "LB", 1.4, 6.0, "S"),
            D("MIKE", "LB", 4.5, 3.2, "M"), D("SS", "S", 4.5, -3.2, "SS"),
            D("LCB", "CB", 1.2, -14.0, "C"), D("RCB", "CB", 1.2, 13.0, "C"), D("FS", "S", 10.0, -1.6, "FS")]
    p = Play(off, bear, los=35, to_go=None)
    # backfield: counter step right, then the handoff going left
    go_to(p, "QB", (-3.9, -0.4), kind="path", speed=3.5)
    go_to(p, "RB", (-4.4, -0.9), kind="path", via=[(-6.6, 1.2)], speed=3.9)
    go_to(p, "RB", (5.6, -5.4), kind="run", via=[(-1.4, -3.4), (0.8, -4.4)], speed=5.6)
    p.handoff("RB", t=1.1)
    # play side: block down
    go_to(p, "LT", (0.2, -2.6))
    go_to(p, "LG", (0.1, -0.7))
    go_to(p, "H", (0.9, -3.3), speed=3.2, delay=0.05)
    # backside: center blocks back, Y hinges on the Will
    go_to(p, "C", (-0.3, 1.1))
    go_to(p, "Y", (0.3, 4.1))
    # the pullers: guard kicks out the end man, tackle wraps through the hole for the Mike
    go_to(p, "RG", (-0.5, -5.4), kind="pull", via=[(-1.6, 1.2), (-1.9, -3.0)])
    go_to(p, "RT", (2.6, -2.0), kind="pull", via=[(-2.3, 2.6), (-2.6, -3.0), (0.2, -3.6)], speed=6.0, delay=0.1)
    # receivers clear the corners away
    p.route("X", r.go(18)); p.route("Z", r.go(18))
    p.man("LCB", "X"); p.man("RCB", "Z")
    # defense
    go_to(p, "WE", (-0.2, -6.0), kind="rush", speed=1.5)
    go_to(p, "WT", (0.6, -2.1), kind="rush", speed=1.2)
    go_to(p, "NT", (0.6, -0.3), kind="rush", speed=1.0)
    go_to(p, "ST", (0.1, 1.5), kind="rush", speed=2.0)
    go_to(p, "WILL", (0.6, 3.9), kind="rush", speed=1.2)
    go_to(p, "SAM", (-1.6, 2.4), kind="rush", via=[(-2.2, 5.2)], speed=4.8)
    go_to(p, "SAM", (-0.6, -1.2), kind="path", speed=4.2)
    go_to(p, "MIKE", (4.3, 4.0), kind="path", speed=3.0)
    go_to(p, "MIKE", (3.6, -1.4), kind="path", delay=0.3, speed=4.4)
    go_to(p, "SS", (1.8, -2.9), kind="path", delay=0.45, speed=4.0)
    go_to(p, "FS", (6.1, -5.4), kind="path", delay=1.0, speed=4.2)
    return p


P46 = one_back_vs_46()


def tags(fld, p, t, i):
    if i == 0:
        say(fld, p, 6.8, 3.6, "both OLBs\nto the TE", color=style.DEFENSE_DARK, fontsize=6.6)
        say(fld, p, -3.6, -5.4, "H-back", color=style.OFFENSE_DARK, fontsize=6.6)


MOMENTS = [
    (0.0, "", "Both OLBs (W, S) are stacked on Y.\nLeft of the ball: E, T, N and SS."),
    (0.45, "counter step", "R jabs right, toward the stack;\nM steps with him. G and T pull."),
    (1.25, "pullers arrive", "G kicks out E; H takes SS;\nT and G block down; C blocks back."),
    (2.75, "through the hole", "T has M. Only FS is left, and W\nand S are chasing from behind."),
]
animation_or_strip(P46, MOMENTS, lateral=(-8.6, 7.0), window=(-8.2, 11.2), width_in=5.8,
                   rings=(("RG", PURPLE), ("RT", PURPLE), ("RB", GREEN)), after=tags)
```


::: {.callout-note title="Film room: Washington 1987 — Super Bowl XXII"}
**The game:** Washington 42, Denver 10, at San Diego on January 31, 1988. Denver led 10–0 after the
first quarter. Washington then scored 35 points in the second quarter, still the Super Bowl record:
Doug Williams, the first Black quarterback to start and win a Super Bowl, threw four touchdown passes
in that quarter alone and finished with 340 yards, and rookie Timmy Smith, making his first NFL
start, ran for a Super Bowl record 204 yards.[^sb22]

**What to notice:** the one-back sets with two tight ends, the H-back moving before the snap, and
Smith's long runs, which come behind pulling linemen after a step the wrong way: the counter trey.
Then watch Ricky Sanders's two touchdown catches in the same quarter, of 80 and 50 yards, and
ask yourself whether you could have told run from pass before the snap. That uncertainty is the point
of the formation.
:::

The rivalry with Ryan went on after he left Chicago to coach the Philadelphia Eagles (1986–1990).
In November 1990 his Eagles beat Washington 28–14 on *Monday Night Football* in the "Body Bag Game,"
knocking nine Washington players out, both quarterbacks among them; eight weeks later, in the wild-card
round in Philadelphia, Washington won 20–6, and three days after that the Eagles fired Ryan.[^bodybag]

## Spreading the field: the run-and-shoot and the K-Gun

By the late 1980s the next offensive answer was simply *more receivers*. If the 46 and the
blitz-heavy defenses of the decade were built to win with numbers near the line, an offense could
take the numbers away by spreading out.

The **run-and-shoot** went furthest: four wide receivers, one back, no tight end, and routes chosen
after the snap from what the coverage did. Mouse Davis and June Jones, its two great teachers,
brought it to the NFL, and between 1989 and the mid-1990s it was the base offense of the Detroit
Lions, the Houston Oilers and the Atlanta Falcons. Warren Moon led the league in passing yards for
Houston in 1990 and 1991. The defenses' answer was the one Ryan always preached: hit the
quarterback. Four receivers meant only five or six blockers, and blitzes that brought more rushers
than that forced the quarterback to throw before the routes had sorted themselves out. Ryan, by then
Houston's defensive coordinator, called his own team's offense the "chuck and duck," and on January
2, 1994 he threw a punch at its coordinator, Kevin Gilbride, on the sideline during a nationally
televised game.[^rns] The language and the reads of the run-and-shoot are in
[Offensive Systems](../04-the-passing-game/04-08-offensive-systems-and-languages.qmd).

Buffalo's version was more durable. The **K-Gun** was a no-huddle offense run with three wide
receivers, one tight end and one back (11 personnel), with quarterback Jim Kelly calling the plays
at the line. Its weapon was the clock between plays. A defense matches the offense's personnel by
substituting when the offense does; when the offense doesn't substitute and doesn't huddle, the
defense has no time to change, and is stuck with whatever it had on the field when the drive started
(the history, including the 1989 attempt to penalize the no-huddle, is in
[In-Game Adjustments and Tempo](../08-the-chess-match/08-04-in-game-adjustments-and-tempo.qmd)).
The 1990 Bills went 13–3, scored a league-high 428 points and beat the Raiders 51–3 in the AFC
Championship Game. They went on to play in four straight Super Bowls, and lost all four.

::: {.callout-note title="Film room: New York Giants 1990 — Super Bowl XXV"}
**The game:** Giants 20, Bills 19, at Tampa on January 27, 1991, decided when Scott Norwood's
47-yard field goal try went wide right with eight seconds left. The Giants were heavy underdogs to
the K-Gun, which had scored 95 points in two playoff games.[^sb25]

**What to notice:** both of the Giants' game plans answer the no-huddle. On defense, Bill Belichick
played extra defensive backs to take away Buffalo's passing game and told his players, who had been
the league's best run defense, that they would win *if* Thurman Thomas ran for more than 100 yards.
Thomas ran for 135 and the Giants won. On offense, Parcells kept the K-Gun on the sideline: the Giants
held the ball for 40 minutes and 33 seconds, still the Super Bowl record. You can't use tempo while
you're standing on the sideline. Belichick's defensive plan is now in the Pro Football Hall of Fame.
:::

## Safe pressure: the zone blitz meets the spread

The spread offenses beat man-coverage blitzes with **hot throws**: when more rushers come than the
protection can block, the quarterback throws immediately to the receiver the blitzer left, and with
four or five receivers spread wide, someone is always open for a moment. The 1990s defensive answer
went back to Arnsparger's idea of safe pressure: rush five, but from places the protection doesn't
expect, and drop a lineman into the throwing lane the quarterback expects to be open. The
[zone blitz](../../appendices/glossary.qmd#gl-zone-blitz) gave a defense the pressure of a blitz
without the man coverage that hot throws punish.

Who invented it is disputed. Some histories credit Arnsparger's Miami defenses, in the 1970s or in
his second stint in the 1980s with the "Killer B's"; others credit Dick LeBeau, Cincinnati's
coordinator from 1984, who studied Arnsparger and turned the idea into a system. This book gives
Arnsparger the idea and LeBeau the system (the case is laid out in
[Zone Blitzes](../07-pressure/07-03-zone-blitz-and-simulated-pressure.qmd)). It became famous in
Pittsburgh, where Dom Capers and LeBeau built "Blitzburgh": the 1994 Steelers led the league with 55
sacks. Capers then took it to the expansion Carolina Panthers in 1995, and in their second season
those Panthers went 12–4 and reached the NFC Championship Game.[^zoneblitz]

Notice the shape of the exchange. The 1978 rules made passing easier; offenses spread out to pass
more; defenses answered by pressuring the quarterback in ways he couldn't read before the snap. It
is the same exchange you'll see again with the spread offenses and two-high defenses of
[The Modern Era](11-05-the-modern-era.qmd).

## 1994: the league tilts the board again

Look back at the points panel of @fig-league-trend. By 1992 and 1993 scoring had fallen to 18.7
points a game, the lowest since 1978, as the zone blitz, better pass rushers and faster defenses
caught up. The owners responded as they had in 1978: in March 1994 they adopted a package of
changes "to increase offensive production." It modified line play, the chucking rules and the
roughing-the-passer rule, adopted the neutral zone infraction (a defender who enters the neutral zone
and draws a flinch stops the play dead), and made two changes that are easy to see on any
broadcast.[^rules94]

**The two-point conversion.** After a touchdown, a team may now try to score two points by running or
passing the ball into the end zone from the 2-yard line, instead of kicking for one. College
football had used it since 1958 and the American Football League all through the 1960s; the NFL waited
until 1994, 24 seasons after the merger, to adopt it. The first one in NFL history was scored by Cleveland's punter
and holder Tom Tupa, running in a faked kick in the opening week of 1994.[^tupa]

The decision is a small expected-points problem, the kind [Expected Points](../13-analytics-and-data/13-02-expected-points-and-success-rate.qmd)
teaches. Kicking was worth almost exactly one point: from 1999 to 2014 (the seasons in nflverse
data before the extra point was moved back in 2015), NFL kickers made 98.8 percent of extra points. Going for two
succeeded 46.9 percent of the time, which is worth 2 × 0.469 ≈ 0.94 points.[^twopt] So on average
the kick was slightly better, and teams went for two only a few times a season each. The two-point
try is a *situational* weapon: late in a game, when the score makes two points worth more than twice
one point, the arithmetic flips, and that is what the coaches' two-point chart in
[Clock and Game Management](../10-situational-football/10-04-clock-and-game-management.qmd) encodes.

**Kickoffs from the 30.** The kicking spot moved back five yards, from the 35 to the 30. A kickoff from
five yards further back lands five yards shorter, so fewer kicks reach the end zone and more are
returned: in 1993 only 68 percent of kickoffs were returned; in 1994, 88 percent. More returns meant
better starting field position for offenses, which is what the package was for. (The kickoff spot went
back to the 35 in 2011, and the kickoff has since been rebuilt entirely; see
[Kickoffs and Returns](../09-special-teams-and-the-rules-that-shape-strategy/09-02-kickoffs-and-returns.qmd).)[^kickoff94]

Scoring rose to 20.3 points a game in 1994 and 21.5 in 1995. The 1978 pattern again: the rules
open a gap, and offenses move in.

## Free agency and the salary cap: changing how teams are built

The last two changes of the era weren't about the field at all, and they may have changed the game
more than any rule about hands. Until 1993, an NFL player whose contract ended could not simply
sign with another team. Through the 1980s the league's rules made movement rare, and from 1989 to
1992 a system called **Plan B** let each team protect 37 players and leave only the rest free to
sign elsewhere. Players sued. In 1992 a federal jury in a case brought by eight players, led by the
Jets' Freeman McNeil, found that Plan B violated the antitrust laws, and in January 1993 the league
and the players settled the remaining suits with a seven-year agreement that rebuilt the system.[^fa]

### Free agency (1993)

[**Free agency (1993)**](../../appendices/glossary.qmd#gl-free-agency-1993) is *the system, in force
since March 1, 1993, that lets a veteran whose contract has expired sign with any team*. Today a player
with four accrued seasons becomes an unrestricted free agent; younger players are restricted, meaning
their old team can match an offer. The first great free-agent signing showed what it could do. Reggie
White, the best defensive end of his era, left Philadelphia in 1993 for a four-year, $17 million
contract with Green Bay that made him the third-highest-paid player in the league, and after the 1996 season he set a
Super Bowl record with three sacks as the Packers won Super Bowl XXXI.[^white]

### The salary cap (1994)

In exchange, the owners got the [**salary cap**](../../appendices/glossary.qmd#gl-salary-cap): *a hard
limit, the same for every team, on what a club may count against its player payroll in a season,
set each year from a share of league revenue*. It began in 1994 at $34.6 million per team, higher than
the expected $32 million because a new television deal with a new network, Fox, raised league
revenue. It is a *hard* cap: no team may exceed it for any reason, and signing bonuses are spread
across the years of a contract so they can't be hidden.[^cap]

::: {.callout-important title="Why it exists"}
The two came as a pair, and each answers the other's problem. Free agency gave players the right to
sell their services to the highest bidder; the cap kept the richest owners from simply buying every
good player, which the league feared would end competitive balance. The trade the players made was
a fixed share of revenue in return for movement; the trade the teams made was freedom to spend in
return for a ceiling that made every contract a choice against every other.
:::

**How the cap changed football strategy.** You will see three of its effects in almost every chapter
of this book.

1. **Positions got prices.** Under a cap, paying one player means not paying another, so teams had to
   decide which positions are worth the most. The answers that emerged in the 1990s still hold:
   quarterback first, then the players who decide whether the quarterback has time, the pass
   rusher and the blind-side tackle. The cap is what turned Lawrence Taylor's effect into a
   salary structure. [Building a Roster](../14-the-business-of-scheme/14-01-building-a-roster.qmd)
   follows that logic to today's contracts.
2. **Rosters churned, so systems had to travel.** With players moving every spring, a team could no
   longer assume its starters had spent five years learning its playbook. Offenses and defenses had
   to be teachable to a newcomer in one off-season, which rewarded concept-based languages (one word
   for a whole pattern, the [Erhardt-Perkins](../../appendices/glossary.qmd#gl-erhardt-perkins) idea)
   and coaches who could install fast. Coaches moved too, and took their systems with them; the
   coaching trees of [Part 12](../12-case-studies/12-01-walsh-49ers-west-coast.qmd) are a product of
   the same mobility.
3. **Depth got thinner, and cheap players got valuable.** A team at the cap can't stockpile veterans,
   so the draft, where players are cheap for their first contract, became the most valuable source
   of talent, and specialists who play only in certain packages (a third-down pass rusher, a nickel
   corner) are bought cheaply rather than kept on the roster as insurance.

The cap also invites accounting creativity. Denver, champion after the 1997 and 1998 seasons, was
penalized twice for how it handled money in those years. In 2001 the league took a third-round pick
over the way the team had funded deferred pay, a dispute that began with deferred payments to John
Elway and Terrell Davis; in 2004 it fined the Broncos $950,000 and took another third-round pick for
agreements, between 1996 and 1998, that deferred players' salaries with interest and so got around
the cap.

## Where the era landed: 1998 and 1999

By the end of the 1990s, each of the era's big ideas had a winner. In 1998 the Denver Broncos went
14–2 behind Mike Shanahan's offense, which married Walsh's play-action passing to the outside-zone
running Alex Gibbs had brought to Denver in 1995 (the story is in
[Zone Running](../03-the-run-game/03-02-zone-running.qmd)). Terrell Davis ran for 2,008 yards, and
John Elway, in his last game, was the MVP of a 34–19 win over Atlanta in Super Bowl XXXIII.[^broncos]
The same season the Minnesota Vikings, with a rookie receiver named Randy Moss, scored 556 points,
then the most in league history.[^vikings] And in 1999 the St. Louis Rams, running Mike Martz's
Coryell-descended offense, the "Greatest Show on Turf," beat the Tennessee Titans 23–16 in Super
Bowl XXXIV.[^rams]

Three champions, three lines of descent from 1978: Walsh's timing game, Coryell's vertical game, and
the run game that the one-back offenses had rebuilt to make both work. Meanwhile the defenses
had their nickel and dime packages, their 3-4 edge rushers and their zone blitzes, and were waiting
for the next rule change. The next round of the story, the spread offenses that came up from
college and the defenses built to stop them, is in [The College Laboratory](11-03-the-college-laboratory.qmd)
and [Dynasties and Counterpunches](11-04-dynasties-and-counterpunches.qmd).

## The whole era on one page

@fig-timeline puts the chapter's moves and counter-moves side by side, year by year. Read across a
row to see what was happening at the same moment, and down a column to follow one side's line of
thought. (Entries not sourced earlier in the chapter come from the Hall of Fame's year-by-year
chronology and the other notes listed here.)[^timeline]

```{python}
#| label: fig-timeline
#| fig-cap: "The arms race, 1972 to 1999. Each row is a year with an important change. Read across for what each side, and the league office, was doing at the same time; read down a column to follow one line of thought. The 1978 row is outlined."
#| code-summary: "Show the Python"
import textwrap

TIMELINE = [  # (year, offense, rules and business, defense)
    (1972, "", "", "Arnsparger's “53”: Matheson rushes or drops; Miami goes 17–0"),
    (1974, "", "Downfield contact limited (the “Isaac Curtis rule”); kickoffs move back to the 35",
     "Fairbanks's Patriots and Phillips's Oilers make the 3-4 a base defense"),
    (1977, "", "One chuck per receiver; head slap banned. Scoring hits 17.2 points a team-game", ""),
    (1978, "Coryell takes over the Chargers", "Mel Blount rule; open-hand pass blocking; 16 games; a seventh official", ""),
    (1979, "Walsh hired by the 49ers; Fouts passes for 4,082 yards", "“In the grasp”: the whistle protects the passer", ""),
    (1981, "Gibbs to Washington: one-back, H-back, counter trey", "", "Lawrence Taylor drafted second overall"),
    (1982, "", "57-day players' strike; a nine-game season", ""),
    (1984, "Marino passes for 5,084 yards", "", "LeBeau becomes Cincinnati's coordinator; zone blitz grows"),
    (1985, "", "", "Ryan's 46: Bears allow the fewest points, win Super Bowl XX 46–10"),
    (1986, "", "Limited instant replay (through 1991)", "Taylor: 20.5 sacks, league MVP"),
    (1987, "Washington scores 35 in one quarter of Super Bowl XXII", "24-day strike; replacement games", ""),
    (1989, "", "Plan B: limited free agency", ""),
    (1990, "Run-and-shoot in Detroit, Houston, Atlanta; Bills' K-Gun scores 428", "",
     "Belichick's plan holds the K-Gun to 19 in Super Bowl XXV"),
    (1993, "", "Free agency begins March 1; Reggie White signs with Green Bay", ""),
    (1994, "", "Salary cap ($34.6 million); two-point conversion; kickoffs back to the 30",
     "“Blitzburgh”: Steelers lead the NFL with 55 sacks"),
    (1995, "Shanahan and Alex Gibbs bring outside zone to Denver", "", "Capers takes the zone blitz to expansion Carolina"),
    (1998, "Terrell Davis runs for 2,008; Vikings score a record 556", "", ""),
    (1999, "Rams' “Greatest Show on Turf” wins Super Bowl XXXIV", "Replay returns, with coaches' challenges", ""),
]
COLS = [("Offense", style.SERIES[0]), ("Rules and business", style.INK_2), ("Defense", style.SERIES[1])]
WRAP, LINE_H, PAD = 30, 0.118, 0.05
rows = [[textwrap.wrap(c, WRAP) for c in (o, rl, d)] for _, o, rl, d in TIMELINE]
heights = [max(1, *(len(c) for c in row)) * LINE_H + 2 * PAD for row in rows]
H = sum(heights) + 0.32
fig = plt.figure(figsize=(6.5, H))
ax = fig.add_axes([0, 0, 1, 1])
ax.set_xlim(0, 6.5); ax.set_ylim(0, H); ax.axis("off")
x_year, x_cols, col_w = 0.05, [0.58, 2.58, 4.58], 1.92
y = H - 0.05
for (name, col), x in zip(COLS, x_cols):
    ax.text(x, y, name, fontsize=8.6, fontweight="bold", color=col, va="top")
y -= 0.27
for i, ((yr, *_), row, h) in enumerate(zip(TIMELINE, rows, heights)):
    if i % 2 == 0:
        ax.add_patch(Rectangle((0, y - h), 6.5, h, fc=style.GRID, alpha=0.35, ec="none"))
    ax.text(x_year, y - PAD, str(yr), fontsize=8, fontweight="bold", color=style.INK, va="top")
    for lines, (name, col), x in zip(row, COLS, x_cols):
        if lines:
            ax.add_patch(Rectangle((x - 0.06, y - h + PAD * 0.6), 0.025, h - 1.2 * PAD, fc=col, ec="none"))
            ax.text(x, y - PAD, "\n".join(lines), fontsize=7, color=style.INK, va="top", linespacing=1.2)
    if yr == 1978:
        ax.add_patch(Rectangle((0.0, y - h), 6.5, h, fc="none", ec=style.INK_2, lw=1.0))
    y -= h
plt.show()
```

## Watch for it on Sunday

::: {.callout-tip title="Watch for it: classic film"}
Find a full game from the 1980s or early 1990s (NFL Films and the league's own YouTube channel post
many; Super Bowls XX, XXII and XXV are easy to find) and chart the first quarter with what you now
know.

- **Personnel and formation.** Count the backs and tight ends on every snap. How often is it the pro
  set or the I with two backs? When does a third receiver appear, and does the defense answer with a
  fifth defensive back? Is anyone lined up as an H-back, a step off the line beside the tackle?
- **The front.** Three linemen with hands down and two standing at the ends (a 3-4), or four down
  (a 4-3)? If you see the center and both guards covered and a safety walked up into the box, you're
  looking at the 46.
- **The best pass rusher.** Find him before the snap. Which side is he on, and what does the offense
  do about it: an H-back next to his tackle, a back staying in, a tight end chipping him?
- **Contact on receivers.** Watch a receiver past five yards. Does anyone touch him before the ball is
  thrown? (After 1978, a flag if they do, but watch how much the officials let go in the 1980s.)
- **The clock between plays.** Does the offense huddle? If it doesn't, does the defense manage to
  substitute?
- **Then flip to a 2025 game** and run the same list. Note what disappeared (the fullback, the 46,
  the huddle on most plays) and what survived (the slant-flat, the counter, the stand-up edge rusher,
  the zone blitz).
:::

## Predict the play

::: {.callout-tip title="Predict the play 1: where does the H-back go?"}
```{python}
#| label: fig-drill-hback
#| fig-cap: "Predict the play 1. 1986: one back, a tight end (Y) on the right, and an H-back who could line up in either dashed spot. The Giants are in a 3-4; their best pass rusher, number 56 (ringed), stands at the end of the line on the offense's left."
#| code-summary: "Show the Python"
# ---------------------------------------------------------------- drill 1: where does the H-back go?
off = line("short") + [O("QB", "QB", -1.9, 0.0, "Q"), O("RB", "RB", -7.0, 0.0, "R"),
                       O("Y", "TE", -0.7, 4.8, "Y"), O("X", "WR", -0.7, -14.0, "X"), O("Z", "WR", -1.5, 13.0, "Z")]
dfn = [D("LDE", "DE", 1.0, T("5", -1), "E"), D("NT", "NT", 1.0, 0.0, "N"), D("RDE", "DE", 1.0, T("5"), "E"),
       D("ROLB", "OLB", 1.2, -6.8, "56"), D("LOLB", "OLB", 1.2, T("9") + 0.3, "B"),
       D("ILB1", "LB", 4.3, -2.2, "L"), D("ILB2", "LB", 4.3, 2.2, "L"),
       D("LCB", "CB", 7.0, -14.0, "CB"), D("RCB", "CB", 7.0, 13.0, "CB"),
       D("FS", "FS", 12.5, -5.5, "FS"), D("SS", "SS", 11.0, 6.5, "SS")]
p = Play(off, dfn, los=40, to_go=10)
p.highlight("ROLB")
fld = draw(p, width_in=6.0, lateral=(-17.5, 16.5), window=(-9.0, 15.0), title=False)
ghost_off(fld, p, -1.5, -4.8)
ghost_off(fld, p, -1.5, 6.4)
say(fld, p, -3.6, -8.4, "H-back here...", color=style.OFFENSE_DARK, fontsize=7)
say(fld, p, -3.6, 9.6, "...or here?", color=style.OFFENSE_DARK, fontsize=7)
say(fld, p, 3.2, -10.8, "the Giants' best\npass rusher", color=style.DEFENSE_DARK, fontsize=7)
plt.show()
```

It's 1986, and your right-handed quarterback is about to face the Giants. They are in their 3-4, and
their best pass rusher, number 56, is standing at the end of the line on your left. You have one
running back, a tight end on the right, and an H-back you can line up on either side. Where do you
put the H-back, and what does he do at the snap?

::: {.callout-tip title="Answer" collapse="true"}
**On the left, next to the left tackle.** Number 56 is lined up over your quarterback's blind side,
so that is where you need an extra man. At the snap the H-back **chips** him: hits him as he comes off
the edge, then releases into a short route if nothing else comes. That gives the left tackle help
against a rusher he can't block alone, and gives the quarterback a check-down when the H-back
releases. This is the job Joe Gibbs created the position for.

On the right, the tight end is already in place to block. If 56 moved to the right side before the
snap, as defenses learned to do, you would want your H-back to go with him, in motion across the
formation. The rule is the one from [Pass Protection](../04-the-passing-game/04-02-pass-protection.qmd):
find the best rusher first and put help where he is, especially if he is on the blind side.
:::
:::

::: {.callout-tip title="Predict the play 2: the K-Gun catches a base defense"}
```{python}
#| label: fig-drill-kgun
#| fig-cap: "Predict the play 2. 1990: Buffalo in the shotgun with three wide receivers (X, H, Z), a tight end and a back, no huddle, against a base 3-4 that was on the field when the drive began. The slot receiver H and the linebacker over him (B) are ringed."
#| code-summary: "Show the Python"
# ---------------------------------------------------------------- drill 2: the K-Gun catches a base 3-4
off = line("short") + [O("QB", "QB", -5.0, 0.0, "Q"), O("RB", "RB", -5.0, 1.6, "R"),
                       O("Y", "TE", -0.7, 4.8, "Y"), O("X", "WR", -0.7, -15.0, "X"),
                       O("H", "WR", -1.5, -8.5, "H"), O("Z", "WR", -1.5, 14.0, "Z")]
dfn = [D("LDE", "DE", 1.0, T("5", -1), "E"), D("NT", "NT", 1.0, 0.0, "N"), D("RDE", "DE", 1.0, T("5"), "E"),
       D("ROLB", "OLB", 2.5, -8.0, "B"), D("LOLB", "OLB", 1.2, T("9") + 0.3, "B"),
       D("ILB1", "LB", 4.5, -2.2, "L"), D("ILB2", "LB", 4.5, 2.2, "L"),
       D("LCB", "CB", 7.0, -15.0, "CB"), D("RCB", "CB", 7.0, 14.0, "CB"),
       D("FS", "FS", 13.0, -4.0, "FS"), D("SS", "SS", 12.0, 6.0, "SS")]
p = Play(off, dfn, los=40, to_go=10)
p.highlight("ROLB", "H")
fld = draw(p, width_in=6.0, lateral=(-18.5, 17.5), window=(-7.5, 15.5), title=False)
say(fld, p, 6.0, -10.6, "a linebacker\non the slot", color=style.DEFENSE_DARK, fontsize=7)
say(fld, p, -4.4, -11.5, "no huddle: the defense\ncannot substitute", color=style.INK_2, fontsize=7)
plt.show()
```

It's 1990. Buffalo gained 9 yards on first down and has hurried to the line without a huddle in the
shotgun: three wide receivers, a tight end, one back. The defense had its base 3-4 on the field when
the drive started, and it hasn't been able to change it. Where will Jim Kelly look, and what should
the defense have done before the drive began?

::: {.callout-tip title="Answer" collapse="true"}
**At the slot receiver on the left (H).** The only player to cover him in a base defense is a
linebacker, the highlighted B, and a wide receiver against a linebacker in space is the matchup
the K-Gun was built to create. Expect a quick throw to H (a slant, an option route that breaks away
from the linebacker's leverage) or a run against a defense with only four defensive backs spread
across the field to cover four receivers.

The fix had to come *before* the drive, because once the offense stops huddling, the defense can only
substitute when the offense does. A defense facing the K-Gun had to start its drives in nickel or
dime and accept the trade: lighter against the run. That is exactly what Belichick's Giants did in
Super Bowl XXV, with extra defensive backs on the field and a promise to let Thurman Thomas run. And
the Giants' offense took away the other ingredient tempo needs: the ball. You can't hurry the next
snap if you aren't on the field.
:::
:::

::: {.callout-tip title="Predict the play 3: before the rule, and after"}
```{python}
#| label: fig-drill-1978
#| fig-cap: "Predict the play 3. Cover 2 against a two-back pro set. The tight end (Y, ringed) runs up the seam between the two deep halves as the Mike (M, ringed) drops to about 8 yards in the middle."
#| code-summary: "Show the Python"
# ---------------------------------------------------------------- drill 3: 1977 or 1979?
off = line("short") + [O("QB", "QB", -1.9, 0.0, "Q"), O("HB", "RB", -5.0, -2.2, "H"), O("FB", "FB", -5.0, 2.2, "F"),
                       O("Y", "TE", -0.7, 4.8, "Y"), O("X", "WR", -0.7, -13.0, "X"), O("Z", "WR", -1.5, 13.0, "Z")]
dfn = [D("WE", "DE", 1.0, T("5", -1), "E"), D("WT", "DT", 1.0, T("1", -1), "T"), D("ST", "DT", 1.0, T("3"), "T"),
       D("SE", "DE", 1.0, T("5") + 0.2, "E"), D("SAM", "LB", 4.0, 6.6, "S"), D("MIKE", "LB", 5.0, 2.0, "M"),
       D("WILL", "LB", 4.5, -3.2, "W"), D("LCB", "CB", 4.5, -13.0, "CB"), D("RCB", "CB", 4.5, 13.0, "CB"),
       D("FS", "FS", 13.0, -8.0, "FS"), D("SS", "SS", 13.0, 8.0, "SS")]
p = Play(off, dfn, los=40, to_go=None)
p.route("Y", r.seam(19))
p.drop("MIKE", (8.5, 3.8))
p.drop("FS", (17.5, -10.0), zone=(8, 14), label="deep half")
p.drop("SS", (17.5, 10.0), zone=(8, 14), label="deep half")
p.dropback(5.0)
p.highlight("MIKE", "Y")
fld = draw(p, width_in=6.0, lateral=(-17.5, 17.5), window=(-8.5, 22.5), title=False)
ruler(fld, p, depths=(5, 10, 15, 20))
say(fld, p, 8.6, -0.8, "M drops to 8 yards", color=style.DEFENSE_DARK, fontsize=7)
say(fld, p, 20.6, 4.6, "Y: seam", color=style.OFFENSE_DARK, fontsize=7, weight="bold")
plt.show()
```

The defense plays Cover 2: two deep safeties and five underneath. The Mike linebacker drops straight
back to about 8 yards in the middle as the tight end, Y, releases up the seam between the two
safeties. What does the Mike do to Y under the 1977 rules, and what can he do under the 1979 rules?
And where is the ball going in 1979?

::: {.callout-tip title="Answer" collapse="true"}
**1977:** nobody touched Y at the line, so the Mike still has the one legal hit the 1977 rule allows,
anywhere on the field (before 1974 he could have hit him as often as he liked). He meets Y at 8 yards, knocks him off his seam, and buys the
safeties time to close the space between them. The route is ruined, and with it the timing.

**1979:** past five yards the Mike may not touch him. He has to turn and run with Y, a linebacker
chasing a tight end up the field, or let him go and hope a safety gets there. Neither safety can,
because each is responsible for his own half of the field, and the seam is exactly between them. The
ball goes to Y at 18 to 20 yards, in the hole that every Cover 2 has in the deep middle.

The defense's eventual answer was to make the Mike *run*: in Tampa 2 he sprints to the deep middle at
the snap, turning Cover 2 into three deep in the middle of the field
([Cover 2 and Tampa 2](../06-pass-coverage/06-04-cover-2-and-tampa-2.qmd)). That linebacker needed
a sprinter's speed, which is one more way the 1978 rules changed what a defensive player looks like.
:::
:::

## Takeaways

- **Two 1978 rules opened the passing game from both ends.** The Mel Blount rule stopped defenders
  from hitting receivers past five yards, which made timed routes possible; open-hand pass blocking
  gave the quarterback more time. Passes went from 40 percent of plays in 1977 to half of them by the
  early 1980s, and interceptions fell for twenty years.
- **The offense split into two answers.** Air Coryell stretched the field deep with protection and
  big receivers; Walsh's West Coast offense stretched it sideways with short, timed throws that worked
  like runs. Gibbs's one-back, two-tight-end offense, the run-and-shoot and the K-Gun built on both.
- **Every defensive answer answered something specific:** nickel and dime for the third receiver; the
  53 and the 3-4 for disguising who rushes; Lawrence Taylor for slow protections; the 46 for two-back
  offenses; the zone blitz for hot throws. Each new answer created the next question.
- **The blind side made the left tackle a premium position,** because a right-handed quarterback
  can't see what comes from behind his left shoulder, and because the best rushers lined up there.
- **The league rewrote the rules again when defenses caught up:** the 1994 package added the
  two-point conversion and moved kickoffs back to the 30.
- **Free agency (1993) and the salary cap (1994) changed how teams are built:** positions got
  prices, systems had to be teachable fast, and cheap drafted players became the most valuable kind.
